course.name: Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II

question.text:
Evaluate the surface integral

\[ \iint\limits_S \left\langle -x, \: -y, \: xyz \right\rangle \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} \]

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=2x+y$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A. \]

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(2x+y) = 2 \\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(2x+y) = 1 \end{align*}

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf F(x,y,z){:}$

\begin{align} \mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) &= \left\langle -x, \: -y, \: xyz \right\rangle \Big|_{z=2x+y} \\[3pt] &= \left\langle -x, \: -y, \: xy(2x+y) \right\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle \underbrace{-x}_{P}, \: \underbrace{-y}_{Q}, \: \underbrace{xy(2x+y)}_R \big\rangle \end{align}

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \left\langle -x, \: -y, \: xyz \right\rangle \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D ( -(-x) \cdot 2 - (-y) \cdot (1) + xy(2x+y) ) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D (2x+y+2x^2y+xy^2) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} (2x+y+2x^2y+xy^2) \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left[ 2xy + \dfrac{y^2}{2} + x^2y^2 + \dfrac{xy^3}{3} \right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left( 2x + \dfrac 12 + x^2 + \dfrac{x}{3} \right) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left( x^2 + \dfrac{7x}{3} + \dfrac 12 \right) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{x^3}{3} + \dfrac{7x^2}{6} + \dfrac{x}{2} \right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 13 + \dfrac 76 + \dfrac 12 \\[5pt] &= 2. \end{align*}

question.text: For a surface $S$ given by $x = k(y,z)$ for $(y,z) \in D,$ the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by \[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \Bigg( P + \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}} \dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y} - R \dfrac{\partial k}{\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}} \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A. \] From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A. \]

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $x = k(y,z),$ it can be parameterized as

\[ \mathbf{r}(y,z) = \left\langle k(y,z),\: y,\: z \right\rangle. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_y & = \left\langle \dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y}, \: 1, \: 0 \right\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_z & = \left\langle \dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z}, \: 0, \: 1 \right\rangle \end{align*}

Now, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_z &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y} & 1 & 0 \\ \dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \left \langle 1, \: -\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y}, \: -\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} \right \rangle. \end{align*}

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(x,y)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_z) \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \langle P, \: Q, \: R \rangle \cdot \left \langle 1, \: -\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y}, \: -\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} \right \rangle \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \Bigg( P + \big( \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}-Q}\, \big) \dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y} - R \dfrac{\partial k}{\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}\partial z}} \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

example.title: Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral Using a Formula

question.text:
For a surface $S$ given by $y = 2xz^3$ for $(x,z) \in D,$ the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by \[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \Bigg( \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\, z^3+Q - \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\, xz^2 \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A. \] From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?

Hint: The orientation of $S$ should be chosen such that the unit normal vector has a positive $\mathbf j$-component.
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A. \] Since our surface $S$ is of the form $y=2xz^3,$ it can be parameterized as

\[ \mathbf{r}(x,z) = \left\langle x,\: 2xz^3, z \right\rangle. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x & = \left\langle 1, \:2z^3, \: 0 \right\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_z & = \left\langle 0, \: 6xz^2, \: 1 \right\rangle \end{align*}

Now, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_z &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 2z^3 & 0 \\ 0 & 6xz^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \left \langle 2z^3, \: -1, \: 6xz^2 \right \rangle. \end{align*}

However, notice that the $\mathbf j$-component is negative. Therefore, we select the normal vector that points in the opposite direction:

\[ \mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_x = - \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_z = \left \langle -2z^3, \: 1, \: -6xz^2 \right \rangle \]

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(x,z)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_x) \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \langle P, \: Q, R\: \rangle \cdot \left \langle -2z^3, \: 1, \: -6xz^2 \right \rangle \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \Bigg( \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}-2P}\, z^3+Q - \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}6R}\, xz^2\, \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

question.text:
For a surface $S$ given by $y = h(x,z)$ for $(x,z) \in D,$ the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by \[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \Bigg( \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}} \,{\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}}+Q - R\,{\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}} \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A. \] From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?

Hint: The orientation of $S$ should be chosen such that the unit normal vector has a positive $\mathbf j$-component.
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A. \]

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $y = h(x,z),$ it can be parameterized as

\[ \mathbf{r}(x,z) = \left\langle x, \: h(x,z),\: z \right\rangle. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x & = \left\langle 1, \: \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}, \: 0 \right\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_z & = \left\langle 0, \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z}, \: 1 \right\rangle \end{align*}

Now, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_z &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \left \langle \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}, \: -1, \: \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right \rangle. \end{align*}

However, notice that the $\mathbf j$-component is negative. Therefore, we select the normal vector that points in the opposite direction:

\[ \mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_x = - \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_z = \left \langle -\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}, \: 1, \: -\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right \rangle \]

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(x,z)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_z) \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \langle P, \: Q, \: R \rangle \cdot \left \langle -\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}, \: 1, \: -\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right \rangle \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \Bigg( \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}-P} \,\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} } + Q -R\, \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z}} \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

example.title: Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral Using a Formula

question.text:
Evaluate the surface integral

\[ \iint\limits_S \left\langle 1, \: 0, \: y \right\rangle \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} \]

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=\cos(x+y)$ for $-\pi \leq x \leq 0$ and $-x \leq y \leq 0.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A. \]

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \cos (x+y) = -\sin(x+y) \\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \cos( x+y) = -\sin(x+y) \end{align*}

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf F(x,y,z){:}$

\begin{align} \mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) &= \left\langle 1, \: 0, \: y \right\rangle \Big|_{z=\cos(x+y)} \\[3pt] &= \big\langle \underbrace{1}_{P}, \: \underbrace{0}_{Q}, \: \underbrace{y}_R \big\rangle \end{align}

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \left\langle 1, \: 0, \: y \right\rangle \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( -1 \cdot (-\sin(x+y)) - 0 \cdot (-\sin(x+y)) + y \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big(\sin(x+y) +y \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi}^{0} \int_{-x}^{0} \left(\sin(x+y) + y\right) \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_{-\pi}^{0} \left[ -\cos(x+y) + \dfrac{y^2}{2} \right]_{y=-x}^{y=0} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi}^{0} (-\cos x + 0 ) - \left(-\cos0 + \dfrac{x^2}2 \right) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi}^{0} \left( -\cos x + 1 - \dfrac{x^2}2 \right) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ -\sin x + x - \dfrac{x^3}{6} \right]_{-\pi}^{0} \\[5pt] &= 0 - \bigg( -0 + (-\pi) - \dfrac{(-\pi)^3}{6} \bigg) \\[5pt] &= \pi - \dfrac{\pi^3}{6} \end{align*}
